rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-3, Tables 4, 8: the authors train their own BLSTM/LSTM/GRU/CNN/MLP/RF models on AquaCrop-simulated tomato and potato yields with 10 years of weather data from Fadagosa, Portugal, and report validation/test MSE and R2.
rows.notes: The study is a yield-prediction modelling exercise: BLSTM predicts end-of-season tomato and potato yield (R2 0.97-0.99) from climate, ETo, soil water content and irrigation amount, with the target yields generated by AquaCrop rather than measured. It never implements or evaluates a precision irrigation scheduling system, and reports no water-use reduction, no comparison with traditional irrigation, and no 30% figure. The only scheduling-type exercise (Algorithm 1, Table 10) applies random irrigation amounts every five days to compute a net return; a reinforcement-learning scheduler is listed only as future work. The yield model is at most a building block (precondition) for a decision system that might later save water.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-3, Tables 4, 8: own model runs (BLSTM etc.) trained and tested on AquaCrop-simulated yields with field weather data from Fadagosa.
rows.notes: No result of the study's own shows that a precision/app-based scheduling system maintains or improves crop yield or quality. The study only shows that a deep-learning model can reproduce AquaCrop-simulated yields under different fixed irrigation depths (MSE 0.017 tomato, 0.039 potato on test set). Yields are simulated, not measured, and no scheduling system is applied to a crop. This is upstream of the claimed effect: a yield predictor proposed as a future component of an irrigation decision system.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2.2 and Table 8: own BLSTM model trained on 45 potato seasons and tested on 20, R2 0.988, using Fadagosa weather data and AquaCrop-simulated yields.
rows.notes: The study reports a potato yield prediction model, not a potato yield increase from a machine-learning irrigation system. There is no 15% yield-increase result, no real-time weather or soil-moisture-driven water adjustment (irrigation regimes were fixed depths every four days or depletion thresholds set in AquaCrop; soil water content is AquaCrop output), and no measurement of tuber size, weight, grade or water stress. The ML-based scheduler is explicitly future work (Section 3, Conclusions). Supports only a precondition (ability to predict potato yield from irrigation and climate inputs).

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-3: own deep-learning model runs on simulated yield data with field weather data.
rows.notes: The study contains nothing on disease, waterlogging or soil aeration. It is a yield-prediction modelling study using AquaCrop-simulated yields on a sandy loam site; no precision irrigation system is implemented and no disease outcome is measured or modelled.

notes: Full text appears complete. Key caveat for all rows: the yield targets, ETo and soil water content used to train and test the models are AquaCrop simulations (Section 2.2, Table 3), not field measurements; the authors acknowledge this (Section 3: 'the models were trained with simulated data'). The study develops a yield predictor intended as a component of a future reinforcement-learning irrigation decision system but never implements or evaluates such a scheduling system, so it provides no own evidence on water savings, yield gains or disease reduction from precision irrigation scheduling.
